cables.q: What if every undersea internet cable snapped at once?
cables.penguin_role: protagonist: the planet's smallest cable-repair technician, hard hat and all
beats: Your messages don't fly through space. They crawl along the bottom of the ocean.
About ninety-five percent of the data between continents runs through cables no thicker than a garden hose. One point four million kilometres of them.
And they break. A lot. Around a hundred and fifty times a year. Fishing gear, ship anchors. Occasionally, a shark.
Usually the internet just reroutes around the damage. You never notice.
But what if every cable snapped at once?
Your local internet would keep working. Anything hosted abroad? Gone. Cloud apps. International payments. Half the websites you use.
And here's the problem. There are only a few dozen repair ships on the entire planet. Fixing every break could take months.
In 2022, Tonga lost its only cable for five weeks.
So the internet isn't in the cloud. It's in a garden hose. At the bottom of the sea.

150-200 faults a year, mostly fishing and anchors (ICPC)

gold.q: What if all the gold ever mined were melted into one cube?
gold.penguin_role: villain: a tiny clay penguin who has been quietly stealing gold bars the whole time
beats: Every bar of gold humans have ever mined. All of it. Fits in one cube.
Around two hundred and sixteen thousand tonnes. Melt it down and you get a cube about twenty-two metres wide.
That's smaller than a baseball infield.
Stand next to it and it's about as tall as a seven-storey building.
Thousands of years of pharaohs, empires and gold rushes. One cube.
Gold is so dense that a single cubic metre weighs about nineteen tonnes. That's a dozen cars, in a box you could stand in.
And who owns it? Central banks hold about a sixth. Nearly half is jewellery.
Humanity's greatest treasure is mostly necklaces.
At today's prices, that cube is worth tens of trillions of dollars.
And it would still fit between the bases. Minus a few bars.
verify: about 216,000 tonnes above ground (World Gold Council, end 2024)
